claims.text: Sliding of CoCrFeMnNi in an inert or ultra-high-vacuum environment can produce a thin ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface tribolayer.
The near-surface transformation in CoCrFeMnNi includes transient dynamic amorphization.
The stress-induced tribolayer transformation occurs rapidly during sliding.
Initially fine-grained CoCrFeMnNi coatings are more prone to tribolayer formation than initially coarse-grained coatings.
Annealed coarse-grained CoCrFeMnNi coatings do not undergo significant stress-induced dynamic transformation during wear.
The ultra-nanocrystalline or amorphous tribolayer increases local hardness.
The tribolayer distributes the applied load more uniformly.
Formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer is associated with low friction in CoCrFeMnNi under UHV sliding.
Formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer is associated with high wear resistance in CoCrFeMnNi under inert sliding.
Fine-grained coatings will have lower friction coefficients than coarse-grained coatings.
Fine-grained coatings will have significantly lower wear rates than coarse-grained coatings.
An inert or UHV test environment suppresses oxidation and mixed metal-oxide film formation.
Normal loads from approximately 1 N to 10 N provide sufficient mechanical stress to induce dynamic surface refinement in the proposed coatings.
The proposed fine-grain advantage and tribolayer mechanism should persist across the full approximately 1 N to 10 N load range.
Initial hardness and alternative deformation modes may influence friction and wear independently of tribolayer formation.
Residual stresses may influence the observed wear performance.
Failure to observe enhanced tribolayer formation in the fine-grained cohort, or failure of performance improvements to correlate with that layer, is designated as falsifying evidence.

contradictions.description: The design says the cohorts differ only in initial grain structure and that this is the only variable, but the uncertainty field acknowledges potentially influential inherent-hardness and residual-stress differences. Annealing the coarse-grained cohort is not shown to control these possible covariates.
